name: Uma Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Kestrel Electronics, on the business park behind the retail outlet. We make circuit boards for heating controls and smart thermostats. I run a pick-and-place machine, which is a machine that grabs tiny components off reels and places them on the boards, thousands an hour, and then the boards go through the reflow oven to melt the solder. My day is loading reels, checking the first board under the microscope, fixing feeder errors and keeping the line moving.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part you enjoy, and what's the part that drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the puzzles, like when the machine keeps dropping one resistor and you have to work out if it's the nozzle or the feeder or the reel. I've got the AI open on my phone all day, I photograph error screens and ask it what they mean. What drains me is the pay, the shift pattern, and knowing I'm basically one broken car away from a bad month. Dev, my partner, cuts hair at a barber's in town, and we've got about two weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, huh, okay, a bit of an anticlimax. At work I'd joke that I'll keep my job as the human error-code translator. Online I'd maybe post something about how the useful bits of AI are the boring bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the little things I do with AI keep helping and nothing big changes. I'd still be underpaid and stuck on shifts. Honestly I'd be a bit disappointed, I was half hoping the change would open doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep doing my evening course in PLCs, that's the controllers that run factory machines, because the controls engineers get paid properly. I'd keep fixing phones and laptops for people on weekends for a bit of cash. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A tiny bit let down, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you were hoping change would open doors. What doors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ones above me. At Kestrel there's operators, then a big jump to engineers with degrees. I don't have a degree and can't afford one. I thought maybe AI tools would let people like me climb without one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the weekend repair work.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly cracked screens and laptops that won't charge, for neighbours and Dev's customers. I charge less than the shop. It's maybe fifty or eighty a month, but that's our buffer, really.

S0.say: She'd call it an anticlimax and joke at work about staying the human error-code translator. Online she might post that AI's useful parts are the boring ones.
S0.think: She thinks her small AI uses keep helping but nothing big changes, so she stays underpaid and on shifts. She'd be a little disappointed, having hoped change would open doors.
S0.do: Keeps going on the line and continues an evening course in PLCs, the controllers that run factory machines. Keeps fixing phones and laptops on weekends for extra cash.
S0.feel: Calm, a tiny bit let down.
S0.quote: I thought maybe AI tools would let people like me climb without one.
S0.fieldNote: Uma is curious and already uses AI all day, and she saw change mainly as a ladder she can't otherwise reach. Her weekend repair work is her real cushion. She was pragmatic, with no blame towards Kestrel or anyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so let's be the ones who know how it works. At work I'd volunteer for any new system and tell the others it's not as scary as it looks. Online I'd share the courses and tools that actually helped me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do okay. Pick-and-place is already automated, what's left is the troubleshooting, and that's my favourite bit. The people I'd worry about are the hand-solderers and the packers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the PLC course this year and ask my manager straight out for a line technician role. I'd suggest to Kestrel that we use an AI camera for the first-board check, because I've already tested one on my phone. If they wouldn't pay me more for it, I'd look at the bigger electronics plant across the county.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, quite good. Nervous about money, like always, but more excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd suggest an AI camera for the check you do now. Doesn't that cut your own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It cuts the boring part. I'd rather be the person who set it up than the person who got replaced by it. That's my whole approach, really, be next to the machine, not in front of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the hand-solderers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd help them if they wanted. Grace on the rework bench is brilliant with a soldering iron, better than me. But she says she 'doesn't do apps'. I can't make her, I can only offer.

S1.say: She'd say the change is coming, so workers should be the ones who understand it. She'd volunteer for new systems, reassure colleagues and share useful courses and tools online.
S1.think: She believes she'd do well, since the remaining work is troubleshooting, which she loves. She worries more about hand-solderers and packers.
S1.do: Finishes her PLC course this year and asks for a line technician role. Proposes an AI camera for first-board checks, which she has already tested, and would look at a larger plant if Kestrel won't pay more.
S1.feel: More excited than worried, though nervous about money as always.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the person who set it up than the person who got replaced by it.
S1.fieldNote: Uma would happily automate part of her own job, framing it as being 'next to the machine, not in front of it'. Her only worry is money, not the change itself. She spoke warmly of an older colleague who refuses apps, without judging her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone, and we need a safety net quickly, whatever it's called. I wouldn't take a side, I'd just say both companies and government have to move. I'd share practical stuff, like how to use the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a shock, because my plan was being the human who works with the machines. If AI can troubleshoot and robots can change the reels, that's me gone too, just a bit later than Grace. And two weeks of savings doesn't buy much time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still try to grab a technician role straight away, because there'd be a rush to install everything, and someone has to be on the floor for that. I'd double the weekend repair work and use AI to find any paid installation jobs going. Dev and I would cut back hard and maybe move in with his brother to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. My stomach goes cold. I'm used to being the one who's ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years' warning, does being an early adopter help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year, maybe. I'd be useful during the installing. After that, I'd be in the same queue as everyone. Being early only helps if there's somewhere to be early to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to Dev's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Haircuts, I'd guess, last longer. People like a person with scissors. So maybe he carries us for a while, which would be strange, because I've always been the planner.

S2.say: She'd say it's too fast for anyone and a safety net is needed quickly. She'd avoid taking sides, saying both companies and government must act, and share practical advice.
S2.think: It's a shock because her plan relies on being the human who works with machines, which AGI would replace too. Two weeks of savings buys little time.
S2.do: Seeks a technician role at once to ride the installation rush, doubles her weekend repair work and uses AI to find paid installation jobs. Cuts back hard with Dev and considers moving in with his brother.
S2.feel: Scared, with a cold stomach, unused to falling behind.
S2.quote: Being early only helps if there's somewhere to be early to.
S2.fieldNote: Uma's confidence cracks when even troubleshooting is automated, and she said so plainly. She still acts fast, aiming to ride the installation rush. The idea of Dev carrying the household reverses her usual role and clearly unsettled her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get ready, if we start now. At work I'd push people to learn the new systems while the jobs still exist. Online I'd keep sharing what's working for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me a proper window. Factories would spend three or four years installing robots, and they'd pay technicians well to do it. I could make real money and save some before the end point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my PLC certificate in the first six months, then move to a technician job, even if it's further away. I'd save hard, aiming for three months' cushion by year three. I'd keep the repair work going and maybe turn it into a small proper business with a stall at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but sharp. Like a deadline I can actually work towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why turn the repair work into a business if robots can do repairs too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people still want to hand their phone to a person and hear 'it'll be fine.' Maybe that lasts, maybe it doesn't. But it's a second leg to stand on, and I've only got one right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in year five itself, when it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea, honestly. I'd have savings and skills, but if the AI does the skills too, then I'm just someone with savings. I'd hope by then the government has worked out the money side.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now, urging colleagues to learn new systems while jobs last. She'd keep sharing what works for her online.
S3.think: She sees a window of three or four years where factories pay technicians well to install robots. She thinks she could earn and save real money before the end point.
S3.do: Earns her PLC certificate within six months and moves to a technician job, even further away. Saves towards a three-month cushion by year three and grows her repair work into a small business with a market stall.
S3.feel: Nervous but sharp, like a deadline she can work towards.
S3.quote: If the AI does the skills too, then I'm just someone with savings.
S3.fieldNote: Uma treats the five-year version as an earning window, much like a contractor would. She was candid that she has no plan for the year AGI arrives. She is building a 'second leg' through her repair side business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for everyone to adjust sensibly. Companies, schools, government, all of it. I'd be telling everyone at Kestrel to start learning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is good for me. I'd have time to become a controls engineer, maybe even part-time study for a diploma. The end point still worries me, but I'd be in a much better spot when it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the five-year one, PLC first, then technician, then a two-year technical diploma at night. I'd build the repair business slowly and get Dev and me to six months' savings. I'd also learn whatever AI systems come out each year, because that's half the fun for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A low hum of worry, but I'd feel ready rather than chased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything ten years lets you do that five doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Study properly. With five years I'd grab the quick money. With ten I could do the diploma and become someone the company really needs, not just someone handy. That's a different kind of person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any plans with Dev?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about buying a small place someday. With ten years and steady savings, maybe around thirty-two. I wouldn't take on a big mortgage though, not knowing what work looks like after.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is enough for companies, schools and government to adjust sensibly. She'd urge everyone at Kestrel to start learning now.
S4.think: She thinks ten years suits her, giving time to become a controls engineer through part-time study. The end point still worries her, but she'd be better placed.
S4.do: Gets a PLC certificate, moves to a technician role, then studies for a two-year technical diploma at night. Builds the repair business slowly, reaches six months' savings with Dev and keeps learning new AI systems each year.
S4.feel: Mostly fine, with a low hum of worry, feeling ready rather than chased.
S4.quote: I could do the diploma and become someone the company really needs, not just someone handy.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Uma would choose deep study over quick money, which she framed as becoming a different kind of person. She'd consider buying a small home but avoid a big mortgage. She enjoys new AI tools, which shapes her optimism.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it skips the bit where people like me are useful. What would help is fast, paid technician training for operators, and some kind of income guarantee while things settle. Not a handout forever, just something to stand on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people like about their jobs. I love the puzzle of a machine that won't behave. If AI takes the puzzles too, I'd need to find puzzles somewhere else, and I'm not sure where.

headlineQuote: That's my whole approach, really, be next to the machine, not in front of it.
portrait: Uma is a 27-year-old pick-and-place operator at a circuit-board factory on a business park, living with her partner Dev, a barber, on about two weeks of savings and a small weekend phone-repair income. She uses AI all day, is studying PLCs at night, and hopes technology can be the ladder her lack of a degree blocks. Pragmatic and unbothered by politics, she sees steady change as good for her and would automate parts of her own job. Fast AGI shakes her because it removes the window where people like her are useful, while ten years feels like enough to study and become someone the company truly needs.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it skips the period when people like her would be useful.
whatWouldHelp: Fast, paid technician training for operators and a temporary income guarantee while things settle, not a permanent handout.
